item.title: Growing Requires Growth: Building the Systems Behind CEA’s Community Expansion
item.description:
Published on August 17, 2026 8:42 PM GMT

I love EA; I am really proud of what we have built at CEA, and I am excited about where CEA is heading- that is all still very true. And after taking time to step back and think about where I most want to direct my energy next, I made the bittersweet decision to move on from CEA. I have spent my entire (!) full-time career there. I so deeply admire my stellar coworkers, and I deeply love EA and the impact we have- that is a big part of what made this decision so hard. I also still think it's the right decision for me.

Earlier this year, I drafted the following post about my experience leading the talent growth pillar at CEA but didn’t end up posting it. It's a nice reflection on the past year and highlights some of the amazing work of others and the things we have built that will be here long after I leave. So I am sharing it now (even though some of it is quite out of date).

I will also use it as a chance to advertise that we are hiring for a Director of Community Growth, which will oversee both my previous portfolio (Groups, Courses, Online) and Events (EAG, EAGx, Summits, Meta-coordination forum). I think this is an insanely impactful combined portfolio and encourage people to apply or send referrals. 

Just under a year ago, I transitioned from my previous job as Head of Groups into my current role as Director of Community Growth at the Centre for Effective Altruism. At the start of 2025, our engagement metrics were declining. I had never led a cross-functional strategic initiative like this before, nor led a team to build a strategic growth model from scratch. Now, I manage the Groups, Online, and Courses Teams (roughly doubling the number of people under me), and we have grown engagement with CEA programs by 25%. We plan to continue growing and are actively hiring.

Growth has now become my thing and, importantly, not just the growth of EA. To grow participation in our programs, three types of growth had to happen in tandem: I needed to expand our infrastructure, my team, and myself.

Of course, my experience is anecdotal and won’t generalize everywhere, but I have personally found reading reflection posts like this helpful in the past. I wanted to share some key takeaways from what worked for me, in hopes of helping other organizational leaders who are ambitious about their growth. This also gives me a chance to shout out some of the amazing people I get to work with.

 

 

1. Growing Infrastructure

When we shifted from team-level goals to an org-wide growth ambition, we needed different infrastructure. CEA had tried various approaches over the years, but they weren't a good fit for the scale of what we were now trying to do. Sustainable, quality growth requires both systems to track what's happening and frameworks to make good decisions.

  • Building Measurement Systems and Frameworks: 
    • You can’t measure growth unless you know what you are actually measuring. You need to measure something. At the start of the process, I was overwhelmed by the option space - there were so many possible metrics, and they were all far from perfect. Would picking these specific metrics mean we wouldn't focus on the most important things? There was so much they didn't capture!
    • We ended up designing a 6-tier growth funnel to track engagement across all stages of an EA user journey. Alex Dial led the methodology work: figuring out how to work with messy data and making tough calls about which imperfections to accept.  Because no metric is perfect or "non-goodhartable," we introduced the GROW principles. These cultural principles help steer the organization towards impact instead of just optimizing metrics. Our engagement funnel gave us shared language and actual goals to hold ourselves accountable to, and a cultural framework ensured impact-focus. 
    • Ultimately, slightly imperfect goals are better than no goals at all, especially when paired with guardrails, cultural principles, and a concrete plan to improve the model over time. Accepting this allowed us to move forward without letting perfect be the enemy of the good.
  • Driving Accountability Through Goals:
    • A big focus for me was championing goal-driven management across CEA. There are many approaches to OKRs. Historically, some teams at CEA had taken more of a Google-style approach: you should hit about 80% of your goals, and if you're hitting more than that, you're not being ambitious enough. But in practice, this meant we didn't have a strong culture of accountability for the most important goals. We didn't have clearly enforced must-hit targets or shared language around that standard. And many teams were creating independent goals rather than backchaining from CEA-wide goals (and some teams didn’t have goals at all!).
    • Setting must-hit targets (and building a shared language around what "must-hit" actually means) was critical for creating shared expectations that we really do need to run through walls for these. 
    • Mid-year, we were uncertain whether we'd hit our growth targets. At our team retreat, I had to deliver that news and rally the team to refocus. Repeated, clear communication about where we stood and where we needed to go kept everyone aligned when it would have been easy to drift.
    • I have found it particularly exciting to watch Sarah Cheng lead her team to become extremely good at hitting must-hit targets and set a good example for the org.
  • The Product Mindset and Foundation Building: 
    • At one point last year, I really started grokking just how ambitious we could be if we set some audacious goals. Building scalable products people love requires testing assumptions and building feedback loops. If we want to build really scalable products, we need to build a lot of infrastructure. You have to make sure you have products that people really love, that have the effect you want, and that are scalable. That takes quite a bit of work - testing your assumptions, iterating, building feedback loops.
    • For a while, we had vaguely wanted a product mindset at CEA, but we didn't have a playbook or a clear picture of what it would actually mean for what we do. I didn't know where the best starting points were. Last year, I hired Jamie Harris, who had experience with product development. He brought a product lens that reshaped how our team thinks about scaling, and he's now leading the foundational product work at CEA, which is driving internal resource allocation. For example, instead of immediately trying to scale our current products, such as our opportunities board, we are taking the time to really understand our target audience, market size, user needs, and a path to efficient scaling.

 

 

2. Growing My Team

One of the highest-leverage actions you can take is to multiply your impact by increasing the capabilities of the people you work with. We need a team of great leaders to achieve our ambitious goals.

  • Giving Away My Legos: 
    • To grow the team, I had to give away my "babies" (projects I cared about deeply). For instance, after I set it up, Angelina Li took on project management for our growth initiative and did an excellent job. Similarly, Joris Pijpers has been an absolute champion in taking on my legos, ranging from entire hiring rounds to keeping teams accountable to goals and deadlines. 
    • Real empowerment means letting go, even when you think you could do it faster yourself or feel attached to something you have built. It is incredibly fulfilling to watch those I have handed things off to run with projects and do a much better job than I could have. Handing off these projects has allowed me to think a lot more about cross-CEA strategy this year, which I simply didn’t have time to before. 
    • Kennan McClung has recently taken on a role as Interim Head of Groups. Groups had been my focus for so long, it was really hard letting go here, but I have a lot of trust in Kennan, and this allows the team to have leadership while my focus has expanded. 
  • Coaching, including beyond direct reports: 
    • When the number of people in my purview doubled, it was overwhelming. At any time, there are so many problems to be solved, dynamics to be smoothed, cultures to build, etc. I couldn’t have my eyes on, let alone solve, all the problems. And as I stepped into a cross-functional role, I cared about the outcomes of teams beyond those I directly managed. 
    • One of the best gifts Anna Weldon has given me this year is a coaching orientation. As she states it “let people be the hero of their own story”. I had to create a value shift inside myself from someone who could solve a lot of problems to someone who coaches others to solve problems (and even coaching others to coach others to solve problems). 
    • I've encouraged the people I work with to read the same books as me so we can establish a shared language and paradigm, and I find it really exciting to scope out where someone can grow and the ambitious futures they could achieve. 
    •  In the last year, I have picked up more coaching relationships outside of just my direct reports. Having a dedicated space for coaching calls—focused on people's growth areas and on setting ambitious visions for them has been incredibly high-leverage
    • For example, watching Alex Dial's growth over the past year has been one of the most fulfilling things I've done - going from conversations about extra accountability to watching him independently shape and drive organizational priorities.
  • Ruthless focus:
    • We did not have the capacity to execute our ambitious plans nor hire for that capacity, so we needed to find it within. That meant prioritizing and making tough trade-offs. We took people off lower-priority projects to focus on core bottlenecks, even when it was painful. I ended up using a lot of the Groups team's capacity on Growth, and the Groups team suffered. This was so hard, because I think groups are insanely impactful! If Alex and I had stayed focused solely on groups support, we simply wouldn't have a growth model today. While we have not been able to give as much focused support to groups, the creative growth strategies Alex has developed are significantly influencing organization-wide priorities. 
    • I endorse the tough tradeoffs and the general principle of "If the things you are saying no to aren't painful, you are not prioritizing enough." And now I’ve become a bit of a meme at CEA of being “the focus person” - which I am perfectly okay with.
  • The Power of Vision: 
    • A shared vision empowers a team and creates autonomy. On the Groups team, we were constantly faced with new and exciting options, from student project incubators to internship programs, which led to my spending a lot of time reviewing decisions and weighing in on what we should focus on. Providing a vision allows a team to self-evaluate options by asking, "Is this the highest leverage move to achieve our vision?" For example, our current guiding vision for our pilot university program is “Make sure we have good groups at top universities year over year.” This simple framework helps the team stay focused without me weighing in on too many decisions. It is awesome watching Kennan McClung run with this vision - keeping his team focused and goal-oriented.  

 

 

 

3. Growing Myself

I think having a growth mindset is a superpower, and it's a superpower you can develop. It's probably one of the most accessible superpowers you can get, and it's such an enabler to take on so much more.

When I took on this initiative, I had a lot to learn. Here are a few things that have been helpful for my own personal growth:

Systematized development: I am a personal development nerd. With quarterly OKRs (shoutout to Peter Wildeford and Caroline Jeanmaire’s quarterly planning template!), personal development is built into my weekly planning and manager check-ins. My past personal development goals included many of the things mentioned in this post: 

  • Learning to craft a vision had to start with feeling in my heart the importance of a vision (Leading Change and the Art of Coaching Teams were helpful here) and then systematically, with deadlines, running rounds of iteration, tinkering, and testing with my team to see what works while checking on my progress every week.
  • When I took on growth, I realized that learning to influence across the org would help make growth an org-wide priority, even though I don't manage most of CEA. By consistently returning to this as a personal development challenge, I have been more successful than if I had just run into it without conscious growth. (It turns out the vision work above is very helpful here too!)
  • When you're taking on new challenges and doing things for the first time, disappointments are inevitable; building the grit to move through them quickly becomes essential. I added a weekly reflection question: "What setback did you hit, and what did you do to move past it?" Now, I rarely use that prompt since the reflexes have been built.

Constant consumption of information: There are no perfect books, but they can provide lots of helpful tidbits and tools: I listen to audiobooks while doing chores for passive learning and do closer, annotated reads of the "gold" ones. I focused heavily on strategy, management, and product development. Some I have liked specifically include Good Strategy Bad Strategy, Lean Product Playbook, Hacking Growth High Output Management, and as mentioned above, Leading Change and The Art of Coaching Teams. 

  • In particular, I have found these helpful for introducing new frameworks such as for strategic clarity: Doing “strategy” is notoriously difficult. When people say “strategy” they can mean anything from writing a north star vision to mapping all the causal nodes in a space to (my now favorite): identifying one core problem and then creating a set of coherent actions to solve that problem. The combination of reading these books and gaining on-the-ground experience was incredibly helpful in overcoming major hurdles when crafting strategies. I went from seeing strategic work as something that made me doubt whether I could be a good leader to something I thoroughly enjoy and have been told I am pretty good at.

Working with Excellent People: Personal growth is easier when you work with people who challenge your thinking and point out blind spots. I’ve been lucky to check in with Zach Robinson, my manager, and Anna Weldon, who has been coaching me this year.  Amy Labenz has been a powerhouse at CEA who is inspiring to work alongside. Naomi Nederlof has given me excellent feedback that has helped shape my personal development goals for the coming year. I've also learned a great deal from the people mentioned in this post and am grateful for the many wonderful people here.

In a yoga class last year, we had to write a theme for the year on an index card. Mine was simple: 

 

What’s Next

I am proud of the progress we made this year, but we have a far ways to go. We still have gaps in our measurement - conversion tracking, impact weighting, and full user journey mapping across products. We've done some initial work to understand how people move through our programs, but there's a lot more to do. We need to scale our programs. We need to coordinate across an ecosystem. We need to ensure that as we grow, we grow sustainably and maintain the parts of EA that make it great. We need to work on EAs' brand and funding diversification, all while maintaining sustainable momentum. 

We have a lot more infrastructure to build as we scale, and the team will continue to grow in both headcount and skill. I am excited for new challenges and learning opportunities. All three types of growth personal, team, and infrastructure have multiplicative effects and will continue as we systematically invest in these. I'm excited about our new Director of M&E and Strategy being able to put more capacity on this as well as the great talent we aim to hire this year.

EA ideas are too important and impactful to have so few people using them. While EA has significantly punched above its weight for its size so far - the problems we are facing are too big to tackle at this scale. I feel so motivated to help EA grow, and I am lucky to grow it alongside such wonderful people.

item.title: Systemic change and EA: What is it all about?
item.description:
Published on August 18, 2026 6:06 AM GMT

Ever felt like something's missing from how EA talks about “doing good”? Like the conversation stops just short of asking what's actually broken at the root? This opening post introduces a sequence born from exactly that itch: a group of EA-adjacent volunteers who spent three years exploring whether there are systems-level dynamics and interventions that the community should be paying more attention to. 

Post 1: In this first post of our sequence, we set the stage for the empirical and conceptual work to come:  we outline who we are, how our collaboration came about, why we believe systemic change should be more of a focus area within EA and what we are hoping to achieve with this sequence. We hope you consider this as an invitation into an ongoing conversation.

In the coming posts, we will then:

Post 2: Bedazzle you with definitions – what even is “systemic change”?

In the second post of the sequence, we propose an understanding of systemic change-related work that emerged from our internal discussions. Based on that, we outline key criteria that organisations should pay attention to when designing systems-conscious strategies. We offer these as a starting point for discussion across the community and for adaptation by each individual organisation or project.  

Post 3: Excite you with data – do EA organisations actually pay attention to systemic issues already?

In the third post, we describe our empirical investigation. We conducted this in the form of a questionnaire to assess the systems-orientation of existing organisations. We will go into detail on our methodology, present the results from our empirical exercise, and discuss several limitations which reduce the robustness of our findings. 

Post 4: Share our joy and frustration with you – and imagine the future together.

We pick up on these limitations in the last post of the sequence. This post collects open questions, remaining uncertainties, and potential points of contention that we would love to see discussed across the EA community. We close the post with the motivation that started the whole project: our case for an EA-inspired effort to change systems rather than just addressing isolated problems.

Why focus on systemic change?

The case for focusing on the transformation of systems rather than aiming for incremental improvements within a system can be mapped onto cause prioritisation frameworks like ITN or cost-effectiveness analyses, with a slight twist:

Importance

Tackling systemic features that lie at the root of pressing problems is highly important, because such systemic features are often huge levers for improvement. For instance, removing lead from gasoline, water sources, or paint products is a higher-leverage intervention than treating diseases and cognitive impairments after populations have been exposed to lead. Preventing new lead from entering drinking water and other everyday products through changed laws and regulations has even more potential positive impact. At the deepest systemic level, eliminating problems like lead exposure would be achieved most effectively if there were not just new rules but a shift in what societies consider acceptable risks to impose on others. That kind of shift renders it inconceivable for actors to recklessly contaminate living environments in the first place.

Tractability

Tackling systemic issues successfully is moderately tractable. It is true that systems are difficult to understand and predict. Thus, effective interventions are less tractable than they would be for more well-contained, experiment-prone problems. But there are cases of tractable work to promote systemic change. To take just two examples:

  1. Survey research helps to assess the likely success of different mobilisation strategies that social movements use to push for systemic change (Ostarek et al. 2026, Ostarek et al. 2024).
  2. Cash transfer experiments generate evidence about how people might respond if our social and economic system were complemented by Universal Basic Income programmes (GiveDirectly research summary, GiveDirectly list of studies).

Tackling systemic issues is ... possibly neglected? We as the authors of this group share an anecdotal sense that this is the case, especially within and adjacent to the EA ecosystem. Our empirical investigation (read Post 3 of the sequence, forthcoming) gestures in a similar direction: It seems like EA-adjacent organisations consider systemic issues mainly in passing and rarely as their main strategy for impact. But that investigation faced major limitations and is not robust enough to turn our results into strong claims. If you disagree on the neglectedness point, we would love to hear from you down in the comments!

All that said, we believe that the case for a stronger orientation towards systemic change also carries a benefit which is a bit awkward to fit into the ITN framework (and similar cause prioritisation frameworks): An effective change to a systemic structure is sustainable in a way that one-off interventions often cannot be. Even if interventions addressing the symptoms of a problem might perform well on a cost-effectiveness analysis in the short term, their impact might be short-lived. Problems come back when the intervention is scaled back. The flip side to that is that systemic change must be carefully evaluated to prevent sustained negative change that is hard to reverse.  

Looking at systemic change with the help of these criteria (importance, tractability, neglectedness, and sustained impact) suggests that there is more room in the EA ecosystem for approaches that lead to radical change of systems. We advocate for more research and entrepreneurial attempts to further our understanding of how this could be realised and will propose a long-list of solution directions in the final post of this series.

Who are “we”?

We write these posts as private individuals, not as representatives of any of the organisations we are each affiliated with. This project was not backed by any funding and is purely based on volunteer work. We have different levels of engagement with the effective altruism community, but we all share a commitment to the basic principle of using reasoning and evidence to tackle the world’s problems effectively. We also all believe that the effective altruism community has built an impressive space to flesh out, discuss, and act on this principle.

How did we get here?

The idea for this project emerged through many informal conversations. We had these amongst ourselves, with colleagues who collaborated on the project in its earlier phases, and with others in the EA space (at conferences and other social events). In these conversations, we noticed that we shared a sense of dissatisfaction and confusion about the lack of connections between the EA community and other political and social movements. Many such movements are motivated by similar goals: reduce suffering and increase “moral goods” in the world. But they are often informed by quite different ideas about how to achieve them. More specifically, there is one perspective that seems less prominent in EA than in other movements for doing good. That is a focus on systems dynamics and a goal of tackling problems at the systemic level.

We are aware of previous discussions about systemic change within EA (EA forum posts on the topic, 80,000 Hours). A growing number of political and lobbying-based interventions are already being pursued by EA-aligned organisations. At the same time, significant scepticism remains.   • Could few underlying systemic structures cause most of the problems EAs are concerned about, making intervening directly at the root causes potentially much more impactful?
  • Could short-term, highly impactful interventions be net-negative by ignoring deeper systemic issues? For example, easing immediate harm might support flawed systems and block more meaningful, lasting solutions.
  • What might more systems-aware interventions look like? How could systemic interventions (most of which would have longer feedback loops) be paired, evaluated, and compared to interventions that look promising on short-term metrics?

We felt keenly aware of the risk for such conversations to dissolve into unhelpful infighting, where people talk past each other because they hold starkly different starting assumptions. With this sequence, we hope to help avoid this unproductive outcome. 

We spent the last ~three years investigating what we mean by “systemic change”: We developed a list of criteria to rate organisations based on their level of engagement with systemic issues/considerations, applied these criteria to existing organisations in the EA ecosystem, and analysed the results. All of this aimed to produce a decent empirical overview of the status quo. 

The data from our investigation suggests some differences within and across EA cause areas. However, our findings are limited due to the low reliability between raters and time-constraints on our research. Therefore, we refrain from drawing generalisations from the data and focus on a descriptive analysis instead. We welcome any thoughts or questions in the comments (or via direct communication to ourselves, if preferred)! This sequence is very much meant as a conversation starter. item.title: Two crazy-ish charitable global poverty project ideas
item.description:
Published on August 18, 2026 9:54 PM GMT

I am writing up two charity ideas I’ve wanted to investigate, but haven’t been able to, in the hopes someone will investigate them further. If you end up investigating either, I'd be most interested to see what conclusions you come to!

Vulture preservation as a global health intervention

Since the mid 1990's the vulture population in India has been rapidly declining. The reason is due to a few chemicals which are fed to livestock, which is highly poisonous to vultures.

A paper by two University of Chicago economists came to the surprising conclusion that the decline of vultures increased human mortality by 4% (!!) leading to hundreds of thousands of excess deaths. That number peaked my attention.

After reading it, I reached out to the authors of the paper as well as some people working on vulture preservation in India to learn more.

My takeaway (this was almost two years ago, so my memory is fuzzy) was that the chemicals responsible for the decline of vultures (particularly diclofenac) had cheap alternatives and that lethargy alongside regulation imposing minor switching costs to industry has kept regulation from being taken up and enforced.

By doing LEEP style policy advocacy to adopt and enforce bans on the chemicals responsible for the die-out, one might be able to save many lives. The project would be to find out what regulation is needed, lobby to get it passed, and then lobby to ensure it is enforced.

It’s likely also possible to raise money for this project from conservationists who usually spend their money on things I don’t value much, therefore vastly increasing the counterfactual impact (insofar as you as you share my ethics).

Further research that is needed:

  1. Learning exactly what chemicals are responsible for the vulture die out, which alternatives exist, switching costs, and so forth
  2. Regulatory hurdles. Would a ban instituted at a state or national level? Do such bans already exist? If so are they enforced? If not, why? Any low hanging fruit?
  3. CEA with BOTECs of the value of vulture restoration, campaign costs, chance of campaign success, costs to industry and government, time discounts, and so forth.
  4. A critical read of the study to decide if the excess death estimate holds water, and a projection of how this number extrapolates into the future. My expectation is that widespread improvements to sanitation in India over the last decade would make the effect size much smaller going forward.

Radio infotainment on responsible income planning in developing countries

A recent RCT by Stefan Dercon et al. found that showing people in rural Ethiopia a video of people in similar circumstances to themselves making clever financial and life choices massively increased future-oriented investments down the line compared to people not shown the documentary.

It’s exactly the type of social science study that pattern matches to my “doesn’t replicate” neuron, but the authors of the study are far from idiots and the RCT is well done, and it’s well.. an RCT.

Even with that in mind I think people would be right to feel skeptical of this result. Beware of the man of one study! But there’s another similar result which leads me to believe the RCT really is onto something.

Family Empowerment Media, an AIM incubated charity, creates radio infotainment to encourage contraceptive uptake. Their effect sizes are also totally nutty.

Ever since seeing FEMs results, I’ve wondered:

  1. Is knowledge of contraceptive options / dispelling stigmas & myths highly conducive to behavioral change?
  2. Is infotainment in general just a really really powerful tool to induce behavior change?

This new RCT pushes me over to thinking that it’s probably the case that infotainment is severely neglected as a way to cause behavioral change.

Radio outreach in developing countries is way cheaper than it has any right to be. When people have no money the value of advertising coca-cola is far lower and a juicy arbitrage emerges.

I think there’s a possible charity which develops compelling infotainment on responsible economic planning, which plausibly could become the world’s most cost-effective charity aimed at improving economic conditions.

One possible counterargument is that people have limited attention spans and different infotainment interventions will crowd each other out. Perhaps if you run infotainment about family planning AND financial planning, they start cannibalizing each other's effect sizes.

Whatever gains you see in family planning comes at the expense of financial planning and whatever else you’re informing people about.

IIRC when this was studied in Denmark, it did look like awareness campaigns for eg. driving safely would cause a reduction in traffic accidents, but correspondingly drive up all other causes of mortality.

Nevertheless even if this effect proves significant, there’s a case for pushing down the salience of coca-cola and up the salience of investing in one’s future.

Research questions:

  1. Find an AIM botec of radio interventions and see how they structure their CEAs of radio planning. Estimate effect sizes of radio programming from Stephen Dercon’s RCT and from that create a BOTEC.
  2. Similarly to the vulture intervention, this idea heavily relies on a single study’s results. Beware the man of one study! Do a skeptical evaluation of the whole idea and look for any questionable assumptions.
  3. Speak to FEM’s leadership, ask simple questions like: “what infotainment has FEM found to work best?”, “Do you have one with subtitles I can watch?”.

 

 

Side note: I found this post sitting in my drafts and realized I never got around to completing it. I'm now posting it despite it being much below the quality of writing I usually feel good putting out. If you found this write up worthwhile to read, that's useful feedback for me to lower my bar for what I post.

item.title: WAI is starting Phase 3 of field-building for wild animal welfare science
item.description:
Published on August 19, 2026 9:49 AM GMT

Summary

This post will summarize the trajectory of Wild Animal Initiative’s field-building for wild animal welfare science so far, along with patterns and indicators we want to see more of going forward. Beginning with an initial phase focused on establishing credibility and awareness of the field, through a second phase that has placed more emphasis on the distinctiveness and broad priorities of the field, we are now moving into a third phase designed to consolidate effort and encourage more projects to build on each other, enabling the field to make faster progress towards answers to key questions and potential interventions. This post also covers where our research funding has gone over the past few years and some of the field-building milestones we’re seeing.

 

WAI’s early field-building

Wild Animal Initiative (WAI) launched in early 2019 with the objective of establishing a mainstream scientific field dedicated to the practical study of wild animal welfare (hereafter referred to as “wild animal welfare science” or WAWS). We chose to approach the problem of wild animal suffering through scientific field-building because there were (and remain) many critical questions requiring empirical research before we could know that any wild animal welfare intervention or policy is having a net-positive impact. The study of wild animal welfare requires concepts, methods and skills from both ecology and animal welfare science, but at the time, there were very few scientists studying the welfare of free-living wild animals and there was little crossover between these fields in terms of projects, conferences, or academic programs. Although it would be possible to hire scientists from one of these fields and cross-train them to do research outside of academia (as indeed we do at Wild Animal Initiative on our research team), academic institutions provide a number of efficiencies, such as access to specialized laboratory equipment, field sites, agreements with publishers, and a culture of peer review. By funding academic research, we could take advantage of expertise and infrastructure all over the world, which would also allow us to reach more animals. By helping to coordinate WAWS into a recognized academic field, we could multiply the impact of the research we fund by making its importance clearer to other scientists and decision-makers, and by potentially attracting mainstream funding from universities and agencies to support more WAWS projects.

Our first challenge was establishing awareness and legitimacy of WAWS as a useful, scientifically compelling and tractable area of research. This would attract scientists from adjacent fields to integrate WAWS concepts and methods into their current research, providing experience that would reveal to them and us their level of enthusiasm and aptitude for long-term engagement with the field.

In those first few years, we emphasized areas of overlap with the adjacent fields of ecology, conservation and captive animal welfare science. We asked researchers in these fields to give WAWS a try. For ecologists that meant trying to interpret physiology and behavior in terms of welfare or measuring putative welfare indicators alongside their population and habitat-scale metrics, while for captive animal welfare scientists that meant developing welfare indicators for species with large wild populations or devising new methods to make captive-based welfare assessment methods feasible to apply in the wild. The support of Coefficient Giving, beginning in 2021, allowed us to launch a grants program and enable many more ecologists and captive animal welfare scientists the opportunity to try their hand at wild animal welfare research. This supercharged our field-building work. Beyond the handful of projects we could actually afford to fund, the prospect of receiving a grant incentivized hundreds more researchers to submit proposals engaging with the concepts and methods we wrote about and collaboratively advised them on.

As we started to see repeat grantees and increasingly relevant projects being proposed, we shifted emphasis away from encouraging researchers to ‘try’ WAWS by simply integrating it with their existing research programs, and increasingly emphasized the challenging priority areas and concerns that make the field distinct and will be necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions. See for example the text of our 2023 call for Seed Grant (<$30k) proposals or our most recent (2025) call for proposals.

As someone who has been with Wild Animal Initiative since the beginning (coming from a PhD in molecular ecology and working part-time on academic outreach at Animal Ethics), if you told me back then that this would be the state of wild animal welfare science in 2026, I would be thrilled. Especially in the past year, we have begun to see important external signals of field-building milestones being reached, including:

  • WAI co-organized the 2025 meeting of the UK’s Animal Welfare Research Network, with approximately a third of the conference dedicated to wild animal welfare. We will be doing something similar for the Spanish-language equivalent, RedCIBA, this year, and have been invited to sponsor themed sessions at several other conferences. WAI’s staff researchers have organized workshops and sessions at many other conferences over the years; what is new here is the scale of our involvement and that we are being invited.
  • WAI’s research team was invited to curate a special issue of the highly regarded journal, Integrative & Comparative Biology, focused on wild animal welfare. This is a huge opportunity and a field-building milestone that they noticed WAI’s research and thought that wild animal welfare would be a compelling theme for their readership.
  • We are seeing more collaborations emerge organically among WAI grantees, and concrete interest in establishing WAWS academic institutions. Within the next six months, we expect to support the launch of the first academic center dedicated to the ecological dimension of wild animal welfare, spearheaded by a cluster of WAI grantees and benefiting from university co-funding. This will complement the NYU Wild Animal Welfare Program, which focuses more on policy analysis. Earlier this year, we also made a grant to Scotland’s Rural College (SRUC) to develop a standalone wild animal welfare module that would connect students from their animal welfare and conservation MSc programs, as well as create a wild animal welfare scholarship and fund small student research projects in wild animal welfare.

Our theory of change has always been centered on academic field-building, as we think that is the only way to get research done at scale with the credibility that will be required to bring positive policy attention to wild animal welfare (on that note, we’re excited to work with the new policy-focused CWAW!). However, academic field-building is only a means to an end, and ultimately we will only be able to improve wild animal welfare if the field produces quality research on impactful welfare issues.

 

The foundation of WAWS laid so far

Developing the science necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions that can meaningfully impact most animals is a huge, long-term endeavor, and most of that impact will be felt only after a sustainable, mission-aligned academic field is established. To that end, we have seen meaningful progress through our grants and internal research towards identifying priorities for further, more concentrated research to focus on. Broadly, we categorize these in terms of identifying factors impacting wild animal welfare, developing tools for assessing wild animal welfare at scale (necessary for monitoring & evaluating interventions), and scoping wild animal welfare interventions. I summarize some highlights from each category here, and you can see the broad sweep of WAI’s external grantmaking allocation in Figure 1 below.

Measuring wild animal welfare

What we haven’t seen enough of

We are happy with the foundation of wild animal welfare research we’ve seeded over the past few years, and excited to see those projects’ results. Funding wide early was a strategic choice, since our first priority was introducing new people to the field and demonstrating its scope and relevance across many disciplines. If our initial priority of establishing mainstream acceptance of WAWS was phase 1 of WAI’s strategy (~2019-2023), and phase 2 involved emphasizing the distinctiveness of the field by leaning more into our priority themes while still focusing on growing the field (~2023-26), we are now entering a third phase. To accelerate progress improving wild animal welfare by building on this initial foundation of research initiatives, and to encourage long-term commitment to WAWS by reinvesting in the researchers who have demonstrated enthusiasm and aptitude for WAWS, the next phase of WAI’s strategy will emphasize the development of research programs over individual projects, and developing institutions through networks of researchers.

(Incidentally, we recently funded a welfare indicator validation project for snails!)
  • For better-understood taxa and contexts, a Seed Grant may not be necessary and a researcher can proceed directly to the first major grant type, a Validation Grant (<$200k). These projects will be entirely focused on testing the validity of potential welfare indicators through a structured process originally proposed by Heather Browning and applied by WAI’s Research Manager Michaël Beaulieu and others (e.g. Beaulieu 2024). These grants will focus on assessing how wild animal welfare is affected by ecological factors, such as resource availability, disease, etc., within particular ecosystems. The objective of these grants is to gradually build up a picture of the causal network of factors so that interventions or policies can eventually be devised to improve wild animal welfare.
  • Intervention Grants will support that final step, and will debut next year, with our 2027 call for proposals. Currently, we do not have these pieces in place for any wild animal welfare intervention, although we have funded projects working towards a foundation for testing a few potential interventions, including rodent fertility control and bird feeding. Investing in WAWS institutions, particularly research centers, could also help accelerate research feedback loops, since co-located wild animal welfare scientists should be relatively up-to-date with each other’s findings.

Conclusion

WAI’s first 7 years of field-building for wild animal welfare science has laid the foundations of a recognized and growing field (albeit one still almost fully dependent on WAI for funding). We have prioritized establishing awareness and legitimacy for the field, publishing research that articulates key concepts of the field, and awarding research grants that showcase the scope and priorities of the field while giving scientists from adjacent fields an opportunity to incorporate wild animal welfare into their personal research programs. A trade-off of this approach is that research has been less concentrated towards any single breakthrough or intervention. However, we are already seeing this pay off in terms of a broad base of interest and support for wild animal welfare science. Our grants have seeded many compelling avenues for further development, and we think the field has reached a stage where WAI-funded research effort can become more consolidated into projects that build on one another. This is a tactical evolution to help ensure the coordination-related benefits of an academic field are actually realized in terms of research towards the most pressing and action-relevant questions.

item.title: Thoughts on Taking OpenAI Foundation Funding
item.description:
Published on August 20, 2026 1:00 PM GMT

In May 2025 I met Yo Shavit, who was working on national security policy at OpenAI and was thinking about how to prepare for a future in which models could seriously assist attackers in creating pandemics. We had a call, and when I shared notes with my team their main response was: "maybe start with not making models that can do that?"

Which is, in many ways, fair: by continuing to push the frontier in biological capabilities, OpenAI's actions were making things worse on many of the problems SecureBio is trying to solve. But OpenAI stopping wouldn't have resolved the problem: other firms were pushing quickly too, and the economic incentives strongly favored rapid capability advancement. Making the world more resilient to pandemics needed to be a high priority regardless, especially in light of models' increasing ability to help people with biology.

When I thought about what our initial conversations might turn into, however, my primary concerns were whether that might (a) compromise SecureBio's ability to independently assess and criticize OpenAI's work or (b) make the world less safe via reducing model developers' motivation to improve safeguards. I do think there's something to both of these, which I get into more below, but it seemed well worth it to talk with Yo about how we could work together.

I explained how we were building an early warning system to flag outbreaks, especially engineered ones that could otherwise spread widely before detection. I described how metagenomic sequencing lets you see what nucleic acid sequences (DNA and RNA) are present in a sample, without choosing in advance which sequences to look for, and how we were piloting this on wastewater and nasal swabs. Over the next few months we discussed opportunities to accelerate our work, he introduced us to OpenAI cofounder Wojciech Zaremba, and both Yo and Wojciech left OpenAI PBC (the for-profit) for the OpenAI Foundation (OAIF). We continued talking to them in these new roles, and these discussions, plus a lot of due diligence, led to the $17.2M OAIF grant which we announced today. I'm incredibly excited about this grant, which will allow us to expand our monitoring system, reduce our turnaround time substantially,[1] and generally reduce the risk that something could spread widely before detection.

Which brings me back to the two concerns I mentioned above. On (a), independence, SecureBio has two divisions, Detection and AI. This grant funds Detection, while the AI side of SecureBio evaluates models from many firms, including OpenAI. The grant does not give OpenAI or OAIF any formal control over what anyone at SecureBio can say publicly about any models. That was important to us, but it was also key to OAIF: Yo was very clear that they did not want to influence SecureBio AI's work, and wanted to review our policies to make sure they were sufficiently robust.

That said, we should pay attention to incentives. While it looks to me like OAIF is making its own decisions, the two organizations are closely linked in a way that goes beyond the shared "OpenAI" name: the OpenAI Foundation's endowment is a ~1/4 stake in OpenAI PBC, and they have almost identical boards. Might the AI side of SecureBio pull punches in criticizing the PBC to increase the chances that OAIF gives Detection more money in the future?

SecureBio has systemic controls to mitigate conflicts of interests, including separate leadership, budgets, and deliverables, and the AI team has written up public docs on their principles and conflict of interest policy. But I think the strongest evidence here is from April, when the AI team was looking at GPT 5.5. The grant was at what I would consider its most sensitive stage: we had been working on it for months with very positive signals, but we still didn't have an answer. This was public internally, and AI leadership was looped in, but there was never a question of this affecting what the AI team published, and in their assessment they documented a range of concerns. The biggest was that across several benchmarks the model would appear to refuse a dangerous question by deflecting, but actually it would go on to provide the requested information by giving a highly-transferable related solution. On these benchmarks the safeguards were illusory, and the AI team released their evaluation while the grant was pending.

This concern with incentives, however, is not new with this grant. When the AI side evaluates a company's models, that company typically pays for the evaluation. For example, OpenAI PBC covered SecureBio's costs for the GPT 5.5 evaluation above. This is common with AI evals, and it's a tighter connection than this grant because there's no AI-Detection division insulating evaluators from financial incentives.

Still, this is a place where it takes continued effort to uphold standards, and if there's any indication that funding for Detection is being used as a lever to pressure our AI team on evals, I'll say so publicly and use whatever leverage I have to stop it (up to and including resignation). But I'm not expecting this, and I think the real worry is a subtle drift towards being more generous without anyone explicitly asking for anything. This is also a concern with funding from Anthropic employees, since SecureBio also evaluates Anthropic's work (ex). So if you see SecureBio put out anything unfairly positive towards OpenAI or Anthropic, or unfairly negative in overcorrecting for these incentives, please say so.

On (b), the question is whether this will let model developers take more risk. If we help them sleep better at night, knowing defenses are stronger, will they just push ahead faster during the day? I want us to be a complement to the frontier firms' internal safeguards, but what if we become a substitute?

A world sufficiently robust against catastrophic biorisk, where it doesn't matter what models are willing to explain because real-world protections are a full substitute for model safeguards, would be a fantastic place to be. We and many other projects are working towards that world! But there's a ton of work to get there. The worry is that AI firms perceive risk as lower and ease up on their safeguards when the risk is still unacceptably high.

I think this is directionally real, but as a direct substitute it's small compared to the reputational, legal (liability + risk of directives), and moral forces pushing firms to invest in safeguards. This grant will allow us to flag attacks earlier, but doesn't come close to mitigating the full impact of an attack and only covers one of several paths to large-scale biological harm. The first-order positive effects of making the world more robust to catastrophic biorisk are really very likely to outweigh the second-order effects of reducing safeguards; if I thought the other way around it would suggest that I should instead do or fund work (virus hunting?) that visibly increases risk in order to motivate others to step up, which seems like a terrible idea.

Separately but relatedly, there's also a "political cover" angle, where the PBC might point at this grant (even though it was made by OAIF) to say that they're doing something, taking off some external pressure. To the extent that this reduction in pressure lets them avoid costly actions that would do more to reduce risk, this is a loss, and it's my largest concern with this grant. Philanthropic funding should not be a license to act recklessly, and if they offer it as an excuse we shouldn't accept it. Please keep the pressure on OpenAI, and all the other frontier firms, to slow down and prioritize reducing the risk that their work leads to catastrophe. Even more important than pressuring firms, however, is advocacy for thoughtful AI regulation: this is a coordination problem where it's not in any individual firm's interest to slow down even though it is in humanity's interest collectively.

On balance I think this grant is strongly positive, and I'm much more worried that we won't do the best possible job pushing this work forward than that our efforts will let OpenAI and others ease up on their own work.

    Allowing me to finally answer a question that I asked four years ago, a few months before I quit Google to join the project.

item.title: Effective Altruism and End-Times Fascism
item.description:
Published on August 19, 2026 9:58 PM GMT

I just read an article from The Guardian, written in April 2025 (I'm a bit behind on my reading ...). It's a good read, but that's noy why I share it here. What I want to highlight is something I'm seeing more and more, which is very negative portrayals and stereotyping of EA. 

Some EA's seem ok with this, or accept that it goes with the territory. I vehemently disagree. I would argue that bringing EA thinking to the centre of the Overton window would be the single most impactful achievement of the 21st century, and that it is something we need to take very seriously, and dedicate resources to.

 The rise of end times fascism | Far right (US) | The Guardian

This particular article is about the evil and danger of the fascist right-wing that is sweeping across the US and much of Europe. About a world in which empathy is seen as a great weakness, a world in which those opposing a climate armageddon are equated with Satan, a world of self-styled "Christian nationalism," where foreigners are enemies whom we torture to inspire the loyalty of the masses, ... well, you know, the world many of out elected leaders seem to inhabit. 

Then, while reading and sadly nodding my head in agreement with so much of the article, I came upon this text:

 "There is also effective altruism and longtermism, both of which skip over redistributive approaches to helping those in need in the here and now in favor of a cost-benefit approach to doing the most good in the long term. Though they can appear benign at first glance, these ideas are shot through with dangerous racial, ableist and gender biases about which parts of humanity are worth enhancing and saving – and which could be sacrificed for the supposed good of the whole. They also share a marked lack of interest in urgently addressing the underlying drivers of collapse – a responsible and rational goal that a growing cohort of figures now actively shun."

Those EA's who live in EA-bubbles probably do not realise just how badly EA is perceived in mainstream media. But this is The Guardian, a very liberal UK newspaper, and the article was written by two very well known liberal activists, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. On almost any political or social question, The Guardian might be the world newspaper most aligned with EA's positions. But even there, this criminally false stereotyping of EA passes. If we were Donald Trump, we would sue for $10 billion for reputational damage, but we'd actually win.

And this is far from a one-off. Just this week, The Economist, another quite liberal outlet, published an article (paywalled) in which EA thinking was described as just "weird" and ideas like direct giving were ironically described as "exotic." And, of course, as usual, the first actual EA person named, the typical EA whose goal is to live a life of luxury but assuage their conscience through public displays of charity, was SBF. That is literally how many people see EA's.

 

Why does this matter?

Effective Altruism is a rare philosophy with the explicit goal of helping people and animals without any strings attached. You don't have to believe in bizarre metaphysical theories (but it's ok if you do). Everybody is welcome. You just need to want to help people and animals as much as you can. 

I don't need to convince this audience that EA is great...

The world would be so much better if everyone were exposed to this thinking in a positive way. But too many people either never hear of it at all, or hear about it as some weird nerdish cult. If you were to ask Americans which public figures might be EA's, they would probably name some of the most evil but clever humans who have ever lived, like Peter Thiel or Elon Musk. That's how EA is perceived, and that's why it's so hard to spread our message.

We need people to start thinking of typical EA's as more like Peter Singer or Rutger Bregman, who openly focus on helping and caring. Ir we could move the image of a typical EA closer to someone like Mr. Rogers or even Keanu Reeves, that would help balance things a bit and show the caring side that is often overlooked. 

Maybe we could even get some very popular people who are widely respected as decent people (George Clooney, Taylor Swift, Bruce Springsteen, Barack Obama, even Bono ...) to start speaking about EA in a positive way. 

It's easy to ignore this - we work away in our dark corner, not looking for respect or admiration, just doing what is right and helping people. We get to feel like martyrs, which is nice. But unfortunately, if we remain a tiny minority, we will always have limited impact, while those who know how to do PR (often the populists) will continue to move the world in the wrong direction.

IMHO, people across the rich world are struggling to find a philosophy that contradicts the horrific ideas they hear from Trump, Farage, Meloni, Vox, AfD, Orban, ... and they are struggling because so many politicians and parties (all the EPP aligned parties across the EU, the Democrats in the US) that should be providing that alternative have also moved far to the right and accepted many of the neofascist ideas so deeply that they are now considered moderate. 

EA has the potential to offer a clear view which matches with the true worldview of many people, including not just liberals but decent conservatives and true Christians. We don't have to be a political party, we just need to get the ideas out there, being discussed and given a fair hearing, rather than being dismissed as they are today. 

If we can get people asking themselves seriously if they would like to live in a world governed by EA thinking, I believe many would, because at heart people are good - we just need to give them the chance to show their true nature.

item.title: College EA Meetups Everywhere: Call For Organizers
item.description:
Published on August 20, 2026 11:02 PM GMT

This is a cross-post from Astral Codex Ten, Scott Alexander's Substack. Original post here.

There are ACX meetup groups in cities around the world. Every fall and spring, I make a Meetups Everywhere post to try to signal-boost and support them. This summer, I want to focus on college effective altruist groups in particular.

Many colleges[1] have effective altruist meetup groups or clubs. They range from fun social gatherings of like-minded individuals, to serious organizations working hard to build a better world; most are both at once. Published on August 21, 2026 9:36 PM GMT

Why I favor fallibilism over cluelessness

I’ve long been struck by a structural commonality between radical skepticism and cluelessness worries. Since the EA Forum has been discussing cluelessness this week, I figured I’d take another stab at explaining why I don’t find it a credible concern. (Too late to qualify for the official contest, alas.)

Skeptical Burdens

Open-minded people may be tempted by a discourse norm on which we should treat our interlocutors as epistemic equals in a sense that requires us to refrain from holding to conclusions that we cannot prove to their satisfaction. A striking thing about philosophy is that you soon learn that this discourse norm would prevent you from having almost any beliefs at all. A “radical skeptic” who doubts the existence of the external world, or the past, or the principle that the past is some guide to the future, cannot be logically compelled to abandon his skepticism. So we’d best not pin our hopes on such an impossible ambition. We must settle for merely establishing to our own satisfaction that we can reasonably maintain our beliefs in the face of the skeptic’s contrary arguments. The question is not whether we can persuade him, but whether we are persuaded by him to change (i.e., lose) our minds.

Most philosophers are, of course, not convinced by radical skepticism, for various reasons. (I’ve elsewhere summarized some of the considerations I find most stabilizing. In short, I think it can be worth epistemically wagering on our best chance of being right, even in the face of immense uncertainty. In slogan form: use your best judgment, don’t suspend it!) Cluelessness may have more defenders. But a similar methodological principle holds: In this post I’ll be explaining why I’m not convinced, rather than trying to prove that the proponent of cluelessness must agree with me. (They needn’t.)

Epistemic Difficulty vs Cluelessness

I first want to grant something in the vicinity of cluelessness concerns, by way of an important distinction. The thing I grant: it can be extremely difficult to discern what would be best. Absolutely. We face immense epistemic challenges, and it’s often extremely non-obvious how to resolve them.

If one demands that a solution to cluelessness must show how it’s easy to tell what to do, or perhaps must actually provide the correct answer to whatever difficult tradeoffs you’re struggling with, the most reasonable response will often be, “Sorry I can’t help you with that; I’m not sure either.” I’m often “clueless” in the colloquial sense that I am deeply uncertain about the answer to a difficult empirical question, and not in a position to tell anyone else what they should conclude about it. But I typically don’t doubt that others could reasonably conclude one way or the other, depending on the details of their epistemic position.

So what I typically experience is just ordinary epistemic difficulty, not philosophical cluelessness. In the former case, I haven’t reached a conclusion, and can’t even predict where further investigation would lead me — but I’m open to future clarification. Philosophical cluelessness, by contrast, commits one to the much stronger claim that nobody can (realistically) form any reasonable judgments or expectations about this question, no matter how carefully they investigate it. That’s an extremely strong skeptical claim!

I think it’s really important to bear this distinction in mind. It’s easy to come up with examples that motivate epistemic difficulty: the world is full of difficult questions. But I think it’s wildly premature to close the door on further inquiry by taking full-blown cluelessness as a conclusion settled in advance. We should (ironically) be more uncertain and epistemically humble than that.

DiGiovanni’s Argument

I’ve responded to Lenman’s original cluelessness argument over at utilitarianism.net. Anthony DiGiovanni offers an arguably tighter variant on the EA Forum:

  • Let’s say that we c-prefer A over B if the reason we prefer A is an impartial altruistic comparison of the actions’ possible consequences.
  • P1. Normative premise: To justify c-preferring A over B, it’s not enough to say (e.g.) that A seems heuristically good. Rather, we need to argue that A has higher “expected value” broadly speaking, meaning: In some sense we “expect” that, if we were idealized agents who could aggregate all of A’s and B’s possible consequences into literal EVs, then we’d say A has higher EV. (We ourselves don’t need literal EVs to justify c-preferences, hence the scare quotes.) Otherwise, it’s unacceptably arbitrary to c-prefer A.
  • P2. Conceptual premise: If our understanding of A’s and B’s possible consequences is sufficiently coarse-grained, then we don’t have an argument for “expecting” our idealized self’s EV for A to be higher, lower, or equal to B’s. So A’s and B’s “EVs” are incomparable. In particular:
    • a. Against precise EVs: We shouldn’t represent actions’ degrees of c-preferability with literal precise expected values.
    • b. Against “best guesses”: Even if we don’t use literal precise EVs, we shouldn’t always force ourselves to compare A’s and B’s “EVs”.
  • P3. Empirical premise: Due to unawareness (at least), our understanding of any pair of actions’ possible consequences is indeed very coarse-grained — enough that the conclusion of (P2) follows (i.e., these actions’ “EVs” are incomparable). In particular, the actions’ “EVs” are too severely imprecise to compare them, regardless of whether we (a) formally model these “EVs” or (b) appeal to informal/heuristic arguments.
  • Conclusion: We aren’t justified in c-preferring any action over any other.

It’s a neat argument! But as with Lenman’s, it’s far from clear to me that we should have much confidence in any of the premises, let alone all of them. In the remainder of this post, I want to focus on two pressure points: numerical precision and prospective reasons. But my highest-level claim is that (as with arguments for radical skepticism) we should have less confidence in the conjunction of the premises than in the falsity of the conclusion. (We can, for example, reasonably expect that starting a nuclear war would be impartially dispreferable in prospect. You’ve gone badly awry if you lose sight of this.)

Numerical Precision

DiGiovanni’s case for imprecise credences rests heavily on the intuition that it would be objectionably arbitrary to settle on any precise number given the breadth of our uncertainty in the face of conflicting considerations. I get the intuition: from the inside, I’m not sure how I would go about determining a precise credence in non-arbitrary fashion. But I think this confuses a procedural question (by what process should we settle on a credence?) with the substantive epistemic question of what credence is in fact most warranted. The latter question might have a precise answer even if we can’t easily articulate a general high-level process that will reliably yield this correct answer. (This general phenomenon is familiar from philosophy more generally. There is no general philosophical method that reliably yields true answers. If that suffices for you to rule out belief, then you’re back in radical skeptical territory.)

So I’m inclined to think P2 is false (and certainly reasonably rejectable): in many cases we can reasonably—albeit tentatively—expect “our idealized self’s EV for A to be higher, lower, or equal to B’s,” rather than committing ourselves to incomparability, even when our current grasp of their consequences is quite coarse-grained and incomplete.

Prospective Reasons

Alternatively, if you posit incommensurable values then you should probably reject P1. As Caspar Hare argues in ‘Take the Sugar’ (and his recent book Living in a Strange World), (i) one option can be better in prospect than another, even when you know that, given more information, you would (correctly) regard the two outcomes as incommensurable or on a par; and (ii) in such cases, it’s rational to pick the better prospect rather than deferring to the idealized perspective.

One way Hare argues for this conclusion in LiSW is by appeal to the idea that reasons are contrastive: “A consideration is a reason to do X rather than Y, only if it is something that can be said for doing X, but not for doing Y.” (p. 69)

Cluelessness is not a reason to do one thing rather than another. Nor does it cancel or undermine the force of the knowable reasons we have, e.g., to save a particular person’s life. (It may be reason to believe that if we knew more, our reasons to save this one life would be swamped by other reasons. But outweighing is not undermining: the original reason still retains its original force. And again, since we’ve no grounds for expecting the balance of unknown reasons to count against rather than for our currently-preferred action, the fact of cluelessness is normatively inert: it makes no difference to our reasons for action.)

In the absence of competing reasons, impartial concern (regarding the consequences for individuals) should lead us to prefer to save someone’s life rather than have them die prematurely. This remains true even if we have no expectation that a more-informed agent would necessarily concur. (We’d better not expect them to have the reverse preference, of course, but we may expect them to be overwhelmed by incommensurability without being so overwhelmed ourselves.)

Or, as I previously wrote in response to Lenman:

Lenman distinguishes the “visible” (epistemically accessible) and “invisible” (entirely unknowable) consequences of an action. Using this distinction, there is a very quick argument that saving lives has positive expected value. After all, if we’ve no idea what the long-term consequences of an action will be, then these “invisible” considerations are (given our evidence) simply silent—that is, speaking neither for nor against any particular option. So the visible reasons win out, unopposed. For example, saving a child’s life has an expected value of “+1 life saved”, which doesn’t change when our long-term ignorance is pointed out.

It’s less straightforward when we see a range of considerations and just aren’t sure how to weigh them. (Perhaps you’ve heard that clearing forests to create factory farms might sufficiently reduce insect numbers in the area as to result in a net reduction in suffering, but you aren’t sure how credible the claim is, or even how likely it is that insects have net-negative lives on average.) I can then no longer say, in schematic terms, what the “correct” EV is in such a case: it’s rather a judgment call. That brings us back to the earlier point about “epistemic difficulty”—still not the same thing as strict cluelessness.

The Value Correlation Thesis

Finally, I want to wrap up by proposing a principle that helps a lot with general cluelessness concerns, and I think warrants tentative endorsement.

Value Correlation: An action’s short-run/visible value is a positive predictor of its long-run/invisible value. Actions that look good on the visible margin are more likely to be good than bad in the long run.

For example, we should expect that saving someone’s life, or increasing people’s capabilities to pursue their own goals and live autonomous lives, is more likely to have positive than negative instrumental effects in the long run. There could be many specific exceptions, of course. (It’s a defeasible default, not a universal generalization.) But we shouldn’t expect that most short-term goods are long-term bad, or vice versa.

This strikes me as a datum of common sense, somewhat akin to expecting the future to be like the past (though obviously change happens, so there are plenty of exceptions there too). Consider, again, whether we should really regard nuclear war as equally likely to prove good in the long run as bad. Other cases are less drastic, but trigger the same principle in miniature. So I think this principle is a reasonable starting point, and indeed more reasonable than the sorts of alternative starting points that lead to radical cluelessness.
